uas_topic: Critical infrastructure; private property; state preemption; park regulation; public body registration; weaponized UAS; civil remedies; penalties
regulated_party: Any person operating a UAS; public bodies
regulated_activity: Flight over critical infrastructure/private property; local ordinance authority
permit_or_approval_required: No (commercial/FAA-authorization exemption, not a separate permit)
summary: ORS 837.372: Class A violation to operate at or below 400 ft AGL over, or allow contact with, a fenced/posted 'critical infrastructure facility' -- a defined list of 14 facility types (petroleum/alumina refinery; electrical power generating facility/substation/switching station/control center; chemical/polymer/rubber manufacturing facility; water intake/treatment/wastewater/pump station; natural gas compressor station; LNG terminal/storage; telecom central switching office; port/railroad switching yard/trucking terminal/freight facility; gas processing plant; radio/TV transmission facility; steelmaking facility using an electric arc furnace; a Water Resources Department high-hazard dam; a fenced aboveground oil/gas/chemical pipeline; correctional/law-enforcement facility) -- absent an applicable exception. The section's 9 exceptions cover: the federal government; a public body; a law enforcement agency; a contractor/agent acting for any of those three; the facility owner/operator; a person with the owner/operator's prior written consent; the owner/occupant of the property the facility sits on; a person with that owner/occupant's prior written consent; and a person operating for commercial purposes in compliance with FAA authorization. ORS 837.370: bars operating a UAS over private property in a manner that intentionally/knowingly/recklessly harasses or annoys the owner/occupant (not applicable to law enforcement acting under 837.335), on a tiered penalty scale -- Class B violation for a first offense, Class A violation with one prior conviction, Class B misdemeanor with two or more prior convictions (at which point the court may impose a no-UAS-possession probation condition). ORS 837.385: vests UAS regulatory authority solely in the Legislative Assembly, preempting local ordinances except for park takeoff/landing rules under 837.387. ORS 837.387 permits a local government to regulate UAS takeoff/landing in its own parks, but any such ordinance must (a) allow utility providers a reasonable ability to use UAS in parks to inspect utility lines, (b) allow public bodies to use UAS in parks for emergency operations, and (c) provide an affirmative defense for an emergency landing when no equally safe alternative exists. ORS 837.360/.362: public-body UAS registration ($10,000 civil penalty for noncompliance; educational institutions register as users rather than per-aircraft, and pay no fee) and mandatory data-use/retention/third-party-storage policies (not private-sector obligations). ORS 837.365: bars operating a UAS capable of firing a projectile, or specifically designed/modified to cause serious physical injury, subject to a narrow notify-and-insure exception (5+ days' advance notice to ODA/OSP/permitting agency, public notice, $1M liability insurance) -- Class A misdemeanor up to Class B felony depending on whether it fires a projectile and causes serious injury. ORS 837.300-.345 (law enforcement agency UAS use, warrants, exigent-circumstances, training) were reviewed and are out of scope for this private/commercial-operator register; SB 1186 (2025 session), which would have modified these law-enforcement provisions, died at sine die on 2025-06-27 alongside HB 3426 -- see OR-002.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Rely on the 837.372(3)(i) commercial/FAA exemption for critical-infrastructure inspection work, but still get written facility-owner consent when it's easy to obtain -- it removes any ambiguity in the field, and the facility category list is broader than 'critical infrastructure' intuitively suggests (it includes steelmaking, gas processing, and LNG facilities, for example). Because local ordinances are narrowly limited to park takeoff/landing, and even those must preserve utility-inspection access, the main site-specific check for most AEC projects is simply whether the launch/land point is in a park -- but see OR-004 for OPRD's own statewide UAS Operation Area rule, which is a separate and more restrictive layer for OPRD property specifically.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Keep FAA authorization and commercial-purpose documentation on file for any critical-infrastructure flight, since the exemption is the operator's burden to establish if challenged. For private-property work, document flight altitude, duration, and purpose to rebut any claim of intentional or reckless harassment under 837.370, and be aware the penalty escalates on repeat allegations even absent a new type of conduct. See also OR-007 (837.375/837.380 civil remedies), which creates separate civil exposure distinct from these criminal/violation provisions.
verification_status: Full current statutory text verified directly against the Oregon Legislature's official ORS Chapter 837 page in this retrofit pass; facility list, exception list, and penalty tiers reconciled line-by-line against the primary text.
notes: Retrofit pass (2026-08-06) substantially expanded this record's summary with the full 14-category critical-infrastructure facility list, the full 9-category exception list, the 837.370 penalty tiers, and the 837.387 required local-ordinance carve-outs, none of which were previously captured in full detail. See new OR-007 for the civil-remedies provisions (837.375, 837.380) that were not previously in this register at all.

source_title: Unlawful interference with aircraft, wildfire suppression, law enforcement, or emergency response by unmanned aircraft
citation: ORS 837.374, as amended by 2025 Oregon Laws c.604 (SB 1125), eff. 2026-01-01 (previously amended by 2023 c.114 and 2023 c.249)
uas_topic: Interference with wildfire suppression, law enforcement, emergency response, and manned aircraft
regulated_activity: Directing a laser at an aircraft, crashing into an aircraft, preventing takeoff/landing, or interfering with wildfire suppression/law enforcement/emergency response
summary: CORRECTED IN THIS RETROFIT PASS: a companion 2025-session bill to the one previously recorded here, Senate Bill 1125 (enacted as 2025 Oregon Laws chapter 604, approved by the Governor 2025-07-24, effective 2026-01-01), restructured ORS 837.374's penalty tiers for conduct that recklessly or knowingly/intentionally causes a UAS to interfere with a law enforcement, firefighting, search-and-rescue, or emergency-response effort. Before SB 1125, that conduct was bundled into the same tier as directing a laser at an aircraft or crashing into one (Class A violation if reckless; Class A misdemeanor if knowing/intentional). SB 1125 split it into its own, more severe standalone tier: reckless interference with those efforts is now a Class B misdemeanor (subsection (2)), and knowing/intentional interference is now a Class C felony (subsection (4)) -- both substantially more severe than the prior bundled tier. Directing a laser at an aircraft, crashing into an aircraft, or preventing takeoff/landing remain at the original Class A violation / Class A misdemeanor tiers. Death-or-serious-injury conduct remains a Class A felony (up to 20 years) regardless of which underlying act caused it, now including this newly split-out interference category by cross-reference. Second-or-subsequent-conviction UAS forfeiture is unchanged. This corrects the prior record, which described a companion bill, HB 3426 -- proposing essentially the identical Class B misdemeanor/Class C felony restructuring -- as having died at sine die on 2025-06-27 and concluded 'not current law.' HB 3426 did die on that date, but SB 1125, a separate vehicle carrying substantively the same change, passed the Legislature, was approved by the Governor on 2025-07-24, and took effect 2026-01-01 -- it is current law as of this retrofit pass. AEC operators working during wildfire season or near an active law-enforcement/SAR/emergency-response operation should treat the elevated Class C felony exposure for knowing/intentional interference as currently in force.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Build active-incident awareness into wildfire-season scheduling: check for TFRs and coordinate with incident command before flying anywhere near a fire, law-enforcement operation, or emergency response, since 'interference' is broadly defined and doesn't require actual contact with another aircraft -- and, as of 2026-01-01, the standalone penalty tier for this conduct is materially higher (Class B misdemeanor reckless / Class C felony knowing-intentional) than the general laser/crash/takeoff-prevention tier.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document pre-flight airspace/TFR checks for any job scheduled during fire season, and train field crews that felony-level exposure now attaches to knowing/intentional interference with these specific efforts (not just to conduct causing serious injury) as of the SB 1125 amendment's 2026-01-01 effective date -- update any pre-2026 client-facing compliance materials that still describe this as a failed 2025 bill.
verification_status: Full current statutory text verified directly against the Oregon Legislature's official ORS Chapter 837 page, and the enrolled 2025 Oregon Laws chapter 604 (SB 1125) PDF verified directly against oregonlegislature.gov, in this retrofit pass. This corrects a materially outdated conclusion in the prior research pass, which tracked HB 3426's failure but missed SB 1125's passage of substantively the same change.
notes: IMPORTANT CORRECTION (2026-08-06 retrofit): the prior record's 'not current law' conclusion for this penalty restructuring was incorrect -- a different bill (SB 1125) achieved the same substantive result and is now in force. This is a reminder that a 'died in committee' finding for one bill number does not establish that the underlying policy change failed; always check the current codified statute's own amendment history (the bracketed chapter/session-law citations at the end of the ORS section) before concluding a proposed change did not become law.

citation: OAR 736-010-0040(13) (Permanent Administrative Order PRD 4-2026, filed 2026-04-30, agency-approved 2026-04-22)
revision_date: Adopted 2026-04-22; filed 2026-04-30 (CORRECTED in this retrofit pass -- previously misdated as a 2025 adoption)

regulated_party: UAS operators on OPRD land/ocean shore
requirement_type: Prohibition with designated-area exception and permit pathway
permit_or_approval_required: Permit required for takeoff/landing outside designated UAS Operation Areas
summary: CORRECTED AND SUBSTANTIALLY EXPANDED IN THIS RETROFIT PASS: the prior record cited this rule only as 'OPRD administrative rule (adopted 2025, effective May 1, 2026)' with no OAR number; the actual Permanent Administrative Order (PRD 4-2026, amending OAR 736-010-0040) was agency-approved 2026-04-22 and filed with the Secretary of State 2026-04-30, not adopted in 2025 (2025 activity was the rulemaking/comment process, not final adoption). OAR 736-010-0040(13) prohibits UAS takeoff/landing on OPRD-administered property (including the entire public ocean shore under the 1967 Beach Bill) except wholly within a designated 'UAS Operation Area,' and requires FAA-compliant, reasonable/prudent operation that does not harass wildlife. The director/designee may designate, modify, suspend, or rescind Operation Areas (park-wide or partial, year-round or conditional) based on safety/resource/conflict/operational factors, and must publish area maps and conditions at least 30 days before a designation takes effect (except emergencies). OPRD may require a 'UAS Pass' for a given Operation Area and cap daily use. Overnight-use facilities, areas within a half-mile of a federally or state protected area boundary that explicitly prohibits UAS takeoff/landing (absent the adjacent land manager's permission), and any area closed by other statute or rule are permanently ineligible for Operation Area designation. Public-safety agencies and utility providers may operate UAS during emergencies without prior approval, and may operate for non-emergency official purposes with advance notice to OPRD (no permit required for that narrow category). Violation is punishable up to a Class A violation. Critically for AEC work, subsection (14)(j) requires a special use permit for 'commercial or research purposes on any portion of park property' -- meaning a permit is required for AEC commercial UAS work even inside a designated UAS Operation Area, where recreational flyers do not need one; only recreational use is permit-free within a designated area. Effective 2026-08-08, OPRD opened an initial list of roughly 19 park properties (across its Mountain, Valley, and Coastal regions -- e.g., Sumpter Valley Dredge, Bald Peak State Scenic Viewpoint, L.L. Stub Stewart State Park day-use area, Manhattan Beach and Bob Straub State Recreation Sites) as UAS Operation Areas for recreational (non-permit) use; additional sites are being evaluated and will be posted 30 days before opening.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not assume a designated UAS Operation Area means permit-free access for AEC work -- subsection (14)(j) requires a special use permit for any commercial or research UAS use anywhere on OPRD property, including inside a designated Operation Area; the area designations only remove the permit requirement for recreational flyers. Check the current OPRD UAS Operation Areas list (stateparks.oregon.gov) and the half-mile federally/state-protected-area buffer before scoping any coastal, dune/erosion, or beach-access project, and build special-use-permit lead time into every OPRD-property schedule regardless of location.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Start with the site manager or permitting office for Oregon Parks and Recreation Department (OPRD) before scheduling fieldwork, because property-specific conditions may control the route and timing. Request the current form, lead time, fee, insurance and FAA-document checklist, and site restrictions, then keep the signed approval and conditions in the mission file.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain the permit approval (or documentation that the site is within a designated Operation Area) in the project file before mobilizing a crew; treat overnight-use facility sites as an absolute exclusion with no permit workaround.
verification_status: Full current rule text verified directly against the Secretary of State's Permanent Administrative Order PRD 4-2026 filing (OAR 736-010-0040) and OPRD's own state-parks.oregon.gov drone-operations page in this retrofit pass; corrects the prior record's adoption date and adds the OAR citation, which the prior pass did not have.

citation: OSBEELS 'Unmanned Aircraft Systems & Land Surveying Regulations' brochure; regulatory authority under ORS ch. 672 and OAR ch. 820 (Engineering and Land Surveying)
binding_level: Nonbinding guidance interpreting binding licensing statute
uas_topic: UAS-specific licensing-board guidance for surveying/photogrammetric mapping
regulated_party: Persons/firms performing UAS-based surveying or photogrammetric mapping in Oregon
regulated_activity: Practice of photogrammetric mapping and land surveying using UAS
permit_or_approval_required: Professional registration (PLS or Certified Photogrammetrist, as applicable) required for regulated practice
summary: VERIFIED DIRECTLY AGAINST THE PRIMARY PDF IN THIS RETROFIT PASS (previously only confirmed via a secondary mirror). OSBEELS's brochure confirms UAS/drones are a recognized tool for licensed land surveying and photogrammetric mapping in Oregon, and warns that providing photogrammetry/mapping services without proper licensure -- knowingly or unknowingly -- can result in fines or further legal action. It lists five specific 'potential areas of infraction for UAS owners' operating without a license: photogrammetric mapping, topographic mapping, volume computation, 3D mapping, and boundary surveys. The brochure defines a 'registered professional land surveyor' as a person registered and holding a valid Oregon certificate to practice surveying, and photogrammetric mapping as evaluating/measuring land through interpretation of aerial/remote-sensing imagery to determine topography, area, contours, and land features (citing ORS 672.002, 672.005, 672.007). To become a professionally licensed Photogrammetrist, an applicant must meet an approved education/experience combination under OAR 820-010-3010, pass the NCEES Fundamentals of Land Surveying examination, and pass the Colonial States Boards of Surveyor Registration (CSBSR) Photogrammetry examination. The brochure separately points to OAR 820-010-1000 (engineer qualifications) and OAR 820-010-2000 (land surveyor qualifications) for those professional tracks, and references 'Oregon House Bill 4066' as a resource for the state's UAS definition.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Pull the current OSBEELS brochure directly and use its five-item infraction list (photogrammetric mapping, topographic mapping, volume computation, 3D mapping, boundary surveys) as the trigger checklist for which drone-derived deliverables require registered-professional sign-off in Oregon versus which can be produced without it.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Before relying on an unlicensed or exempt delivery path, give Oregon State Board of Examiners for Engineering and Land Surveying (OSBEELS) a written description of the proposed UAS-derived product, its stated accuracy, and whether it will establish or certify boundaries, elevations, or authoritative locations. Ask the board to confirm the applicable license, responsible-charge, certification, or exemption path and retain the response with the project quality plan; the research packet does not establish a UAS-specific turnaround time.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Board-issued practice guidance is a strong indicator of how OSBEELS would evaluate a complaint, even though it is nonbinding — cite it in internal compliance documentation, but confirm current content directly with the Board before relying on specific thresholds in a client contract.

source_title: Civil Remedies for Unmanned Aircraft System Interference and Repeat Trespass Overflight
citation: ORS 837.375 (Interference with an unmanned aircraft system; unauthorized control); ORS 837.380 (Action by owner of real property; Attorney General)
revision_date: 2025 Edition (current); unchanged in the 2025 legislative session
uas_topic: UAS interference civil liability; private-property overflight civil trespass action
regulated_party: Any person (837.375); any person or public body operating a UAS over private property (837.380)
regulated_activity: Intentionally interfering with, or gaining unauthorized control over, an FAA-licensed or government/law-enforcement-operated UAS (837.375); repeatedly flying a UAS over privately owned/occupied real property after the owner/occupant has objected (837.380)
requirement_type: 837.375: statutory minimum civil liability of not less than $5,000 to the UAS owner, plus mandatory reasonable attorney fees to a prevailing plaintiff, for intentionally interfering with or gaining unauthorized control over an FAA-licensed UAS or one operated by U.S. armed forces, a federal agency, or a federal/state/local law enforcement agency. 837.380: a property owner/lawful occupant may sue a UAS operator (person or public body) who has flown over the property on at least one prior occasion after being told the owner/occupant does not want the UAS flown over the property; treble damages plus injunctive relief for a prevailing plaintiff, with attorney fees recoverable if the amount pleaded is $10,000 or less. Does not apply to UAS lawfully in an airport landing/takeoff flight path, or operated for commercial purposes under FAA authorization (though other civil actions, e.g. invasion of privacy, remain available). The Attorney General may separately bring a nuisance/trespass action on the state's behalf, with mandatory attorney fees if the state prevails.
summary: ORS 837.375 and 837.380, part of the same 'Unmanned Aircraft Systems' subchapter as ORS 837.370/837.372/837.385 (OR-001) but never previously captured in this register, create two distinct civil remedies. 837.375 protects UAS operators themselves: a person who intentionally interferes with, or gains unauthorized control over, an FAA-licensed UAS (or one operated by the military, a federal agency, or law enforcement) is liable to the UAS owner for at least $5,000 plus the prevailing plaintiff's attorney fees -- relevant to an AEC operator both as a potential plaintiff (e.g., a member of the public interfering with a survey flight) and, in principle, as a potential defendant if an AEC crew were to interfere with another party's UAS. 837.380 protects property owners/occupants from repeat UAS overflight: after a property owner or lawful occupant has told a UAS operator they do not want the UAS flown over their property, a second or later overflight exposes the operator to treble damages and injunctive relief (attorney fees recoverable if damages pleaded are $10,000 or less). The FAA-commercial-authorization exception found in 837.372(3)(i) and 837.370 does NOT carry over cleanly here: 837.380(3) exempts commercial-FAA-authorized operation from an 837.380 action specifically, but expressly preserves other civil actions such as invasion of privacy -- so an AEC operator's Part 107 status blocks this particular statutory trespass action but not all civil exposure for repeat overflight after an explicit objection. The Attorney General may separately sue for nuisance or trespass on the state's behalf.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: For any survey/inspection project involving repeat flights over the same parcel(s) -- corridor, pipeline, or multi-adjacent-parcel work especially -- log any objection a property owner or occupant raises about overflight, since a second flight after a recorded objection is the trigger for 837.380 exposure regardless of Part 107 status for other civil theories. Where the FAA-commercial exception does apply to block the 837.380 action itself, still document the authorization, since it does not foreclose other civil claims like invasion of privacy.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Treat 837.380 as a distinct, notice-triggered civil-trespass exposure separate from the criminal/violation provisions in 837.370/837.372 (OR-001) -- it does not require any criminal charge or conviction, only a documented prior objection and a subsequent overflight. Confirm whether a specific project's FAA-commercial-authorization status actually defeats an 837.380 claim (it does, per subsection (3)) versus other civil theories it does not defeat (e.g., invasion of privacy, expressly preserved by the same subsection), before advising a client that Part 107 status resolves all private-property overflight exposure in Oregon.
verification_status: Full current statutory text verified directly against the Oregon Legislature's official ORS Chapter 837 page in this retrofit pass.
notes: New record added in this retrofit pass; these two civil-remedy sections sit in the same statutory subchapter as OR-001's authorities but were not previously captured as a separate register entry, despite direct relevance to repeat-overflight AEC survey work.
